FLASHCARD SET · AGES 2 YEARS

Emotions & Feelings flashcards.

Twenty feeling faces for learning the words that go with the wobbles. There is no right way to feel and nothing to fix on these cards — you look together, you name the feeling, and your toddler learns that every feeling has a word and a grown-up who listens.

These cards belong to Toddler 7 on the Kiddo School learning path.

THE CARDS

Every card in the set.

Each card has its own page: the picture and short, practical notes for grown-ups — what it is for, how to use it, how to print it. Tap any card to open it.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Make the face together

    Look at the card, then pull the same face in a mirror. Faces first, words second — toddlers understand feelings in their own cheeks before they understand them in words.

  2. 02

    Name feelings when they happen

    When a real feeling shows up, bring the card: "you look frustrated — like this face." Matching the moment to the picture is the whole lesson, and it works in both calm and stormy seconds.

  3. 03

    No feeling is the bad guy

    All twenty cards get played the same way — sad gets looked at as calmly as happy. Toddlers learn that every feeling is allowed and every feeling passes.

  4. 04

    One or two faces at a time

    Start with happy, sad and calm. Big sets are for browsing; small sets are for learning.

      Happy Flashcard for Toddlers

      The first feeling word most toddlers learn, usually said with a grin. This card gives the smile a name, and your toddler's own happy moments give it a hundred chances to stick.

      What this feeling card gives

      Puts the best-known smile into words, so joy gets announced properly.

      Name it together

      When the giggles arrive, say happy softly and let them say it back.

      What your child picks up

      Linking an inner feeling to a spoken word.

      Print it like this

      Print it bright; happy cards get the best colours the printer owns.

      When feelings get big

      If joy boils over, quiet rooms help it settle faster.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Happy lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Sad Flashcard for Toddlers

      Everyone feels sad sometimes — toddlers, grown-ups, the works. This gentle face lets your toddler see sadness on a card, where it is safe to look at and easy to talk about.

      What this feeling card gives

      Makes the heavy, quiet days easier to point at than to carry alone.

      Name it together

      Look at the sad face together and try the word in a whisper.

      What your child picks up

      Reaching for comfort instead of hiding a low feeling.

      Print it like this

      Ordinary paper is fine; sad cards do their work slowly.

      When feelings get big

      Sit down at their height and wait; company matters more than words.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Sad lesson on the Learning Path.

      Angry Flashcard for Toddlers

      Big feelings need big words, and angry is one of the biggest. This card shows the face without the fireworks, so you can talk about anger before it arrives — the best possible time.

      What this feeling card gives

      Hands the family a word for the stormy minutes, so shouting can shrink.

      Name it together

      Pull the angriest face you can, then slowly un-pull it, eyebrow by eyebrow.

      What your child picks up

      Naming a hot feeling early, before it runs the show.

      Print it like this

      Thick paper recommended; angry cards get gripped and waved about.

      When feelings get big

      Keep your voice low and slow; anger borrows your calm.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Angry lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Scared Flashcard for Toddlers

      Everybody gets scared, from two-year-olds to grown-ups, and saying so out loud makes it smaller. The card's wide eyes let your toddler study a scared face with total safety — nobody here needs to be brave.

      What this feeling card gives

      Puts a picture to the shivery feeling so it can be spoken.

      Name it together

      Say scared together in tiny voices until the word feels friendlier.

      What your child picks up

      That naming a fear is the first step to feeling braver.

      Print it like this

      One for the bedroom wall, one for the kitchen drawer.

      When feelings get big

      Never hurry a fear away; sitting nearby is already enough.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Scared lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Surprised Flashcard for Toddlers

      Surprise is the feeling with the best face — eyebrows up, mouth open. It is usually the funniest card in the deck, because toddlers know this feeling well: birthday hats, peek-a-boo, sudden "boo!".

      What this feeling card gives

      Names the gasp moment, so startles become stories instead of tears.

      Name it together

      Open the biscuit tin together and do the biggest gasp your face allows.

      What your child picks up

      Reading faces quickly, a skill every friendship leans on.

      Print it like this

      Full colour if you can spare the ink; eyebrows need drama.

      When feelings get big

      Watch their face first; some children prefer their surprises small.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Surprised lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Excited Flashcard for Toddlers

      The wiggly, bouncy, too-much-energy feeling has a name too. Excited is the feeling before birthday cake and after "we are going to the park" — your toddler lives here most days.

      What this feeling card gives

      Catches the jiggly, can't-sit-still energy and gives it one tidy word.

      Name it together

      Bounce on the spot together, then say excited through the wobbles.

      What your child picks up

      Spotting a feeling in the body before it spills over.

      Print it like this

      A quick home print is plenty; excitement rarely waits for laminating.

      When feelings get big

      Excited bodies settle faster moving, so take the wiggles outside.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Excited lesson on the Learning Path.

      Tired Flashcard for Toddlers

      The droopy face at the end of a big day. Tired is the feeling toddlers fight hardest and show most clearly — and naming it can turn a meltdown into an earlier nap.

      What this feeling card gives

      Explains why evenings fall apart, without anybody being in trouble.

      Name it together

      Yawn together deliberately, then say tired and agree it is nearly pyjama time.

      What your child picks up

      Listening to the body's early warnings, like yawns and heavy eyes.

      Print it like this

      Cut it out after bedtime; tired parents get full credit for trying.

      When feelings get big

      Skip the questions and lower the day's volume instead.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Tired lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Calm Flashcard for Toddlers

      The quiet one — soft eyes, easy face. Calm is a feeling worth naming on purpose, because it is the one toddlers need help finding again after big feelings blow through.

      What this feeling card gives

      Gives slow, quiet moments a word, so peace can be asked for.

      Name it together

      Trace the calm face slowly with one finger and match your breathing to it.

      What your child picks up

      Stillness practised while everything is easy, ready for when it is not.

      Print it like this

      Soft colours on plain paper; nothing fancy is needed here.

      When feelings get big

      Keep one quiet song up your sleeve for wobbly afternoons.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Calm lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Shy Flashcard for Toddlers

      Some days your toddler waves from behind your leg instead of running ahead — that is shy, and it is a completely normal way to feel. This face says: new people take a minute, and that is okay.

      What this feeling card gives

      Makes the quiet observer feel seen, not summoned, in busy rooms.

      Name it together

      Wave hello to the card, wave goodbye, and try a nod in between.

      What your child picks up

      That watching quietly counts as joining in.

      Print it like this

      Two small copies; one for the bag, one for the pocket.

      When feelings get big

      Answer hellos for them if needed; braver days will come.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Shy lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Silly Flashcard for Toddlers

      The tongue-out, googly-eyed card your toddler will request daily. Silly is the feeling of pure play — and naming it gives your toddler a word for the jokes they are already telling.

      What this feeling card gives

      Celebrates the goofy face that gets your child laughed with, not at.

      Name it together

      Take turns doing one silly face each, then name the feeling out loud.

      What your child picks up

      Laughter shared on purpose, a real bridge between people.

      Print it like this

      Any paper works; silliness skips the quality checks.

      When feelings get big

      Proud Flashcard for Toddlers

      The chest-out, chin-up feeling after building the tower or reaching the tap. Proud is a big-kid feeling that toddlers earn honestly, and it deserves its own word.

      What this feeling card gives

      Captures the chin-up minute after a wobbly new skill lands.

      Name it together

      Stand on one foot like a stork and say proud without wobbling.

      What your child picks up

      Noticing personal effort, not just results or applause.

      Print it like this

      Go big if the printer allows; proud faces deserve poster size.

      When feelings get big

      Let them retell the win as many times as they need.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Proud lesson on the Learning Path.

      Worried Flashcard for Toddlers

      The furrowed-brow face for the small might-happens that loom large at two: the big dog, the new bed, the rain. Worried feelings shrink when they get a word and a plan.

      What this feeling card gives

      Names the fidgety feeling that comes with new days and unknown plans.

      Name it together

      Tell the card your worry, then turn it face down and have a snack.

      What your child picks up

      Voicing small fears so they shrink in the open air.

      Print it like this

      Plain paper suits this one; worries need no special equipment.

      When feelings get big

      Offer one small next step, not a whole reassuring speech.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Worried lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Frustrated Flashcard for Toddlers

      The gritted-teeth feeling when the block tower falls again or the zip will not budge. Frustration is constant at two, and this card gives the daily struggle a respectable name.

      What this feeling card gives

      Explains the hot grrr of stuck sleeves and lids that will not budge.

      Name it together

      Do up a fiddly zip slowly, name the grrr, then finish it together.

      What your child picks up

      Pausing inside frustration instead of throwing the whole job away.

      Print it like this

      Card stock if the table gets thumped; this one takes knocks.

      When feelings get big

      Slide the word in gently while the storm is still small.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Frustrated lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Confused Flashcard for Toddlers

      The puzzled face — the "what is even happening?" feeling. Confused shows up when routines change or rules seem to bend, and toddlers wear it openly, which is rather lovely.

      What this feeling card gives

      Shows the frown that means the brain is busy, not broken.

      Name it together

      Try wearing a glove as a hat and let the frown speak first.

      What your child picks up

      Comfort with not-knowing, the honest start of all questions.

      Print it like this

      Print as usual; confusion asks nothing extra of the printer.

      When feelings get big

      Slow your words and your pace; confusion hates being hurried.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Confused lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Bored Flashcard for Toddlers

      The flat, floppy, nothing-is-interesting face. Boredom is real at two, and oddly useful — it is the feeling right before your toddler invents something to do.

      What this feeling card gives

      Names the flat, grey afternoon mood that usually arrives around four o'clock.

      Name it together

      Sigh dramatically at the ceiling together, then see who finds a game first.

      What your child picks up

      Sitting with a flat feeling until an idea turns up.

      Print it like this

      Use scrap paper if you like; boredom is not fussy.

      When feelings get big

      Wait a little longer than feels comfortable before supplying the fix.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Bored lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Hurt Flashcard for Toddlers

      The teary face for the stumbles and bonks of daily toddler life. Hurt is the feeling that needs comfort first and words second — this card exists so the word is ready once the tears settle.

      What this feeling card gives

      Turns the sudden cry into a word that summons the right grown-up.

      Name it together

      Practise the word now, softly, so it is ready for real knees later.

      What your child picks up

      Asking for help with a word instead of only tears.

      Print it like this

      Sturdy paper helps; hurt cards often travel to the park and back.

      When feelings get big

      Holding them comes first; the vocabulary can wait its turn.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Hurt lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Loved Flashcard for Toddlers

      The warm, cosy face for the feeling your toddler knows best of all. Loved is the word for cuddles, tucked-in blankets and being found in a crowd — and saying it out loud is the point.

      What this feeling card gives

      Puts the warmest fact of their life into a word they can hold.

      Name it together

      Squeeze a hand on the walk, once for love, once for you.

      What your child picks up

      Being loved out loud makes the feeling easier to trust.

      Print it like this

      Best on the good paper, kept where the cuddles happen.

      When feelings get big

      On the difficult days, say it twice and hold on longer.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Loved lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Friendly Flashcard for Toddlers

      The open, welcoming face that says hello with the whole body. Friendly is the feeling your toddler brings to the park, the baby group and the dog next door — and it deserves a word as much as the tricky feelings do.

      What this feeling card gives

      Cheers on the small wave that opens friendships before words can.

      Name it together

      Pass the card round the table, and each of you waves it a hello.

      What your child picks up

      Greetings as a way of telling people they matter.

      Print it like this

      Print ordinary size; friendliness never needed enlarging.

      When feelings get big

      A wave counts; the spoken hello follows when it is ready.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Friendly lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Kind Flashcard for Toddlers

      The gentle face for the feeling behind sharing a biscuit and patting the cat softly. Kindness happens dozens of times a day at two — it just rarely gets named. This card changes that.

      What this feeling card gives

      Shows kindness as a doing word, done with hands, not just felt.

      Name it together

      Fetch a clean cloth and wipe the table together, saying kind as you work.

      What your child picks up

      Noticing chances to help, then actually taking them.

      Print it like this

      Spare copies make lovely gifts for grandparents; print two.

      When feelings get big

      Name the kindness the moment it happens, quietly and without a fuss.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Kind lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.

      Brave Flashcard for Toddlers

      The chin-up face for the big moments: the first slide, the loud hand-dryer, the doctor's chair. Brave is not the absence of scared — it is scared, and doing it anyway, which your toddler does more often than anyone notices.

      What this feeling card gives

      Stands behind the wobbly first attempt at anything new and tall.

      Name it together

      Hold hands for the first step up, then say brave at the top.

      What your child picks up

      Doing a scary thing slowly, with company, and calling it done.

      Print it like this

      Tuck it in the buggy pocket before the weekend's big attempts.

      When feelings get big

      Count courage in centimetres; a second look counts as climbing.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Brave lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds class on the Learning Path.
